background.text: Well, I was born in Iran.

background.text: And everybody always says, well, why on earth were you born in Iran? And other than the fact that my parents were there, which is the obvious reason, the story is a little complicated, but I guess it boils down to this. My father, who was a physician, and I had, after finishing his residency, joined the Army. And after a couple years in the Army, he was looking for a job at a major academic teaching institution in the United States. He wanted to do research in his specialty of pathology and genetics. And he could not find a job comparable to his white counterparts. And so he and my mom, who, let's say, very interested in doing things outside their comfort zone, decided to look for job opportunities outside of the United States. And my father landed a job offer at the Namazi Hospital, which was a brand new hospital, hadn't even opened up yet, in Shiraz, Iran, chairing the Department of Pathology. So a job that was not available to him. And he was living in his own country. And so he and my mom picked up and went halfway across the world. And I was the second baby born in the Namazi Hospital. They practiced on some other baby firsts. I can't tell you how that went, but it went okay with me. And we lived there until I was five. And from there, my father started doing research in Iran. And it caught the attention of some folks at the Galton Labs at University College of London. And my parents were beginning to think it was time to start going back home. My mom was there. My father was there. My mother was there. She was homesick for her family. And I think they both missed the United States. And they thought, well, why not take advantage of this job offer to go to the Galton Labs for a year? So off he went there. And from there, he started doing research again. And his research got the attention at some international conference of the dean of the University of Chicago Medical Center. And so he landed a tenured track physician in my mother's hometown in the same neighborhood where my grandmother and her other daughter and our whole extended family lived. And my father used to always say to me growing up that sometimes the shortest distance to where you really want to go means you better be prepared to take the long way around. And they sure did take that long way around. And that's where we lived. But for me, coming to the United States was like going to a foreign country. And I was already kind of shaken up going to London. And then here, my parents are so excited about going back home. But it wasn't familiar to me.
